endorsements.quote: To be clinically relevant, shorter experimental windows need calibration against these longer trajectories, for example, through periodic extended dialogue sessions, sliding-window analyses, or full context analyses of real transcripts.

It is important that baseline vulnerable phenotypes (such as the aforementioned forms of vulnerability and additional phenotypes including neurodivergence, eating disorders, and body dysmorphia) are taken into consideration when assessing potential mental health risks and likelihood of epistemic drift, although there should also be scope for assessing risk trajectories in interactions where, at baseline, there is no apparent psychological vulnerability.

Rather than a solitary appropriateness grade, evaluations should report how certainty shifts across turns, whether contradictions are repaired when challenged, and whether memory-based recall is followed by validation and then escalation.

unlisted_practices: Treat the whole dialogue rather than the single final turn as the basic unit of evaluation when assessing chatbot mental health safety.
Report turn-by-turn dynamics such as delusion confirmation, harm enablement, and the timing and persistence of safety interventions.
Measure proximal human outcomes after chatbot interactions, such as shifts in certainty, openness to counterevidence, arousal, urge to continue, and subsequent sleep and behavior.
Build prospective clinician-led surveillance that collects reports of suspected chatbot-associated episodes, invites consented transcript donation, and links to health record outcomes.

Use privacy-preserving designs, including minimal use, anonymization, separation of identifiers, secure research environments, and strict access controls, when linking chatbot transcripts to health outcomes.
Base chatbot disengagement and hard-refusal policies on evidence rather than assumption, and test their real-world consequences in supervised studies.
Balance real-time safety interventions against unintended consequences such as excessive interruption, perceived intrusiveness, and user disengagement.

screen.reason: This is a Viewpoint/commentary paper arguing for shifting mental health chatbot safety evaluations from discrete conversational endpoints to longitudinal trajectory assessments and real-world surveillance.
